Alignment verification

2000-12-31 23:59:59 UTC | All 35 clickable bodies.

Fresh, separate NASA/JPL Horizons queries use a Sun-centred origin and geometric ICRF/ecliptic J2000 vectors. The app's cached samples use barycentric planets and parent-relative moons. This check therefore also tests the origin conversion, axis mapping and moon-parent reconstruction.

Maximum position difference: 179.516 metres. Maximum direction difference after display scaling: 0.0000000717 degrees (moons checked relative to their parent). Three.js world/local transforms reproduce intended moon positions to floating-point precision. These are results for this instant, not an all-time guarantee or physical uncertainty estimate. Updated JPL solutions and interpolation can both contribute to the difference.

No orbital angle correction was warranted. Positions were retained. Illustrative scale changes each orbital radius separately; it preserves Sun-relative planetary directions and parent-relative moon directions, but not pairwise distances or the full heliocentric arrangement of enlarged moon systems. Body pole directions and surface orientation remain illustrative.

For comparison, match the time, observer, coordinate frame, scale and camera orientation. A rotated screenshot is not evidence of a wrong orbit. The app converts JPL (X,Y,Z) to Three.js (X,Z,-Y), a rotation rather than a reflection.

NASA Eyes: exact requested instant | JPL rendered view from above (one second later: the form has five-minute steps). JPL's image provides a visual cross-check, not verification of every small body. All 35 have individual numerical checks below.
